headline_marked: [[Postgres Creator says LLMs score 0%]] on real-world data warehouse queries
headline: Postgres Creator says LLMs score 0% on real-world data warehouse queries
summary: Turing Award winner Mike Stonebraker reveals that while popular benchmarks show 80-85% accuracy, LLMs achieve 0% on actual enterprise data warehouses.
details: Mike Stonebraker, creator of Ingres and Postgres and a Turing Award winner, has a history of accurate predictions in database technology. He now warns against the hype of "chat with your data" solutions, based on new findings.

In a recent interview, Stonebraker stated that Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve 0% accuracy when tested on real-world data warehouse queries. This starkly contrasts with popular benchmarks like Spider and Bird, which report 80-85% accuracy.

Stonebraker's team tested LLMs on four production data warehouses, not synthetic or academic datasets. Even with Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and other techniques, accuracy only reached 10%, rising to 35% when given exact FROM and JOIN clauses.

He identified four key reasons for this discrepancy. First, enterprise data is not part of the LLM's training set, making it impossible for models to reason about unseen data correctly. Second, real queries are significantly more complex, often 100+ lines of SQL compared to 10-20 lines in benchmarks.

Third, real schemas are often messy, with redundant materialized views and idiosyncratic column names like ZUPPERS_BLAH. Fourth, enterprises have domain-specific concepts (e.g., "J-term" at MIT) that LLMs have never encountered in their training data.

Stonebraker published these findings as BEAVER, an anonymized benchmark of real data warehouses, available on arXiv. He urges AI researchers to test their text-to-SQL models against real benchmarks, not "fake" ones.

Drawing parallels to past tech hype, Stonebraker recalled Oracle's early days, where features were promised but not yet implemented. He suggests a similar playbook is at play today with AI companies shipping demos that don't work in production.

He also referenced his 2004 paper, "One Size Fits All: An Idea Whose Time Has Come and Gone," which argued for specialized database engines over general-purpose ones. Modern examples like column stores and vector databases demonstrate this principle.
Regarding Postgres, Stonebraker acknowledges its strength at the low end but notes its limitations for high-end, petabyte-scale analytics due to lack of column store or multi-node support.
